meta.title: What Elon Musk JUST Pulled Off to F**K the Oligarchy
meta.thread_line: 3 threads · SpaceX buying low-band spectrum to become a US mobile carrier, the carrier-oligopoly pricing 'wedge' it targets (T-Mobile/Mint), and a Tesla solar + Powerwall install review.

snapshot: SpaceX is acquiring **low-band spectrum** (Kevin cites 800 MHz) so Starlink can become a major US mobile carrier — signal that penetrates walls, which satellite-to-phone service lacks today.
Kevin's read: a classic **wedge deal** — Musk attacks the Verizon / T-Mobile / AT&T oligopoly, which he says is 'shaking in their boots'.
His carrier evidence: T-Mobile's ~$140/month premium plan and Mint Mobile's sub-$25 tier ride the **same towers** with similar real-world speeds — a price-discrimination spread SpaceX could compress.
T-Mobile is already a SpaceX partner (direct-to-cell), which Kevin frames as defensive: keep the new entrant close.
Apple also partners with Starlink for space-to-phone; Kevin's guess is that Apple wants its frequent-upgrader buyers to see a connectivity edge.
Kevin **holds SpaceX exposure** in several forms and calls ~$132 a floor where he is bullish; he says SpaceX fell ~32% after IPO, in line with his pre-IPO warning of ~30%.
Side note: a positive Tesla solar + Powerwall install review, with one gripe about visible conduit instead of roof penetration.

themes.title: SpaceX buys low-band spectrum to turn Starlink into a US mobile carrier
themes.lead: Low-band spectrum is the missing piece that lets satellite-fed service work indoors, and it moves SpaceX from phone-feature to carrier.
bullets: Low-band frequencies **penetrate walls and fiberglass**; Kevin says SpaceX's buy is of 800 MHz-class spectrum — the fix for 'it'll never work indoors'.
Architecture as Kevin describes it: satellites link to cell towers and the towers radiate over low band — a hybrid, not satellite-only.
Goal: let Starlink operate as a **major US mobile carrier**; Kevin says he would happily switch his own phone service to Musk.
Apple already partners with SpaceX for direct-from-space phone service, but that needs open sky — useless in a tree well or under snow.
Kevin's Apple thesis: the 20-to-45 yr-old buyers who upgrade every year are the audience for a Starlink connectivity pitch; older buyers keep phones ~4 years.
Kevin's SpaceX stance: bought exposure in several ways, floor ~$132; stock fell ~32% from IPO price against his ~30% pre-IPO warning, and fundamentals have 'substantially improved' since.

quote.text: Elon sees this as a wedge. This is the brilliance of Elon. People don't understand this.

themes.watch: Kevin discloses he has exposure to SpaceX stock 'in many different ways'. He also says the video is not sponsored by any carrier named.

themes.title: The 'oligopolistic monopoly': same network, three price tiers
themes.lead: Kevin argues the big carriers protect margin by selling one network under multiple brands, and that is the spread SpaceX can attack.
bullets: T-Mobile premium plans run about **$140/month** (Kevin pays that; plans from ~$80 depending on data), versus Mint Mobile's dirt-cheap tier of roughly $15 for 5 GB (he is unsure of the exact pricing).
Kevin's test: he uploaded video through Mint and got **speeds as good as T-Mobile's** — 'same tower, same network'; he rejects the claim that cheap tiers get meaningfully lower priority.
Why it persists: a flat $15 tier would pull $60-$80 customers down, so T-Mobile hides it behind a separate brand rather than cutting prices.
Analogy: Kirkland salted nuts at $12.99/lb versus Planters at $18/lb — same product, different label.
T-Mobile was among the first partners of SpaceX; Kevin calls this the incumbent 'partnering with the little guy to maintain control'.
Kevin's network verdict: T-Mobile has the fewest dead spots and fastest service he has used, across five carriers/lines (T-Mobile, AT&T, Verizon, Mint, Google line).
themes.watch: Kevin says T-Mobile offered a sponsorship he ignored, and that he is not sponsored by T-Mobile or Mint; whether cheap tiers get lower priority is his personal test, not a carrier disclosure.

themes.title: Tesla solar + Powerwall: great product and service, one install gripe
themes.lead: Kevin has no complaints on product or service, only on how the conduit was routed.
bullets: Installed Tesla panels plus a **Powerwall**; he says the app is polished, installation and service were 'fantastic'.
Gripe: conduit runs down the outside wall and is painted over rather than going through the roof, because the installer won't flash the roof — he'd call a roofer.
Context: he already runs a separate solar system with German-made cells on his roof for about 8 years.

names.name: Tesla (TSLA)
names.blurb: Customer review of solar + Powerwall install; positive.

takeaways.title: Track SpaceX's low-band deal as the step from phone feature to carrier; indoor coverage is the milestone.
Watch T-Mobile, Verizon and AT&T for price cuts or new cheap tiers once SpaceX service launches.
Compare your carrier plan against its discount brand on the same network before paying a premium.
Note Kevin's ~$132 SpaceX floor as his entry marker, remembering he already holds exposure.
Ask solar installers how they route conduit (roof vs wall) before signing.
